newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian reform payoff from 2000/01 - Costello.
newsitem.headline: Australian reform payoff from 2000/01 - Costello.

text.p: Australian Treasurer Peter Costello on Friday marked the fiscal year 2000/01 as the point when the new conservative government's reforms would begin to pay off and deliver higher rates of sustained economic growth.

The Liberal-National administration wanted to create a volume of private and government saving that would eliminate the current account deficit as a restraint on growth, said Costello, who on Tuesday announced a deficit-cutting budget for the year to June 1998.

The economy has been growing for almost six years since the early 1990s recession and Costello said on Friday the growth will not only continue for years to come but continue at stronger rates than have previously been sustained.
"Looking out to those years to 2000/01, what kind of picture do we see emerging?" he said.

"A picture where we are reducing debt, a picture where the commonwealth (federal government) lives within its means, a picture where we have our public saving, a picture where we can sustain growth a levels which we were unable to do in the 1980s and 1990s," he said.

Reserve Bank governor Ian Macfarlane opened up the possibility of faster economic growth on Thursday by saying the central bank would not hike interest rates merely to hold the economy below some pre-conceived danger speed.

Defining an Australian approach to monetary policy much like that of the U.S. Federal Reserve, Macfarlane said the bank would respond only to the likely direction of inflation, and would be happy to let the economy run fast if it expected price pressures to remain subdued.
The bank can guage future inflation from so-called upstream price data -- such measures as wages growth and the prices of manufacturing inputs and outputs.

The economy grew 3.1 percent between the March quarters of 1996 and 1997 but economists expect it to accelerate to an annual rate near 4.0 percent later this year. The government forecasts an average rate of 3.75 percent for 1997/98.

Since it was elected in March 1996, Prime Minister John Howard's government has injected more free-market competition into the labour market -- probably not enough, according to Macfarlane -- and mounted a massive attack on the budget.
